title: They Slowed Me Down So I Could Hear Myself
subtitle: Houston, Atlanta and Miami
focus: The Third Coast takes the crown: Houston chopped-and-screwed and slab culture, Atlanta bass, crunk and trap, and Miami bass with its Caribbean sound-system family

intro.sub: They Slowed Me Down So I Could Hear Myself

intro.t: Houston. Sunday morning. Ninety-four degrees before ten o'clock, and a storefront church between a tire shop and a taqueria, its door propped open for the breeze. There is no breeze.
Greater True Vine has been expecting a visiting youth choir. A church van pulls up with MT. NEBO YOUTH CHOIR painted down both sides. You can see how it happened.
Praise God, y'all made it! Come in, come in. Youth sit on the left. You eat after service. You eat before service, too, you look thin.
Baby, I know what you are. I'm the one that called you. Anybody who comes through that door gets fed. Sit down.
Long as nobody asks me to sing, I'll be whatever choir they need.
Fun fact - storefront churches have been part of -
Tuesday nods and sits down. She has not posted anything in nine days. She has not said much, either.
In the corner, past the folding chairs, a small man in a flat cap sits at a snare drum on a stand. Two and four, and nothing else, and nothing else is needed.
He has seen the van. He has seen Ruth. He does not look up.
That's Brother Wendell. He'll talk to you after. He won't want to. He'll do it anyway, because I'm going to make him.

outro.t: Midnight on the causeway out of Miami. Lantern's folder rides on the dashboard. Nobody has opened it. Nobody has thrown it out the window, either.
We haven't said anything for forty miles, which at my age is a record.
They slowed me down so I could hear myself. Then they sped me up so I could dance. Then they put me in a trunk and drove me down the coast.
Minneapolis drew me five empty stars. Memphis gave me back my guitar. New Orleans walked me down the street. Side B was the side where I started meeting my people.

gigs.title: Slab Sunday
gigs.blurb: Snare in a storefront church on Sunday morning, the slab line on Sunday afternoon. The Deacon keeps both.

vibe.label: Chopped-and-screwed Southern rap and slow soul

challenge.text: Slow it down so you can hear yourself: one song with no misses.

before.t: Sunday afternoon. A lot off the freeway, and a line of cars polished so hard the sky has to look at itself. Candy paint. Wire wheels that stick out a foot past the fenders.
That's mine. The red one. Don't lean on it. Don't breathe on it. My grandfather's riding with me today.
Marcus pops the trunk and it rises slow as a curtain. Neon inside, speakers, a scroll of gold letters on the lid. And out of it, at sixty-one beats a minute, rolls me.
Slowed down this far, I sound like I am thinking it over. I like it here. Do not tell London.
Deacon sits in the passenger seat with the door open: flat cap, white shirt, brass-band sash, sticks in his breast pocket. He has changed out of church and into church.
Brother Wendell said he'd sit through one set. I said two. We settled on one.
Wendell.
Ruth. You still owe me a dollar.
Sixty years, and that's the first thing out of your mouth.
Been saving it. Mm-hm.
Mr. Arceneaux, the count on the recording - Mother Viola said -
I know what Viola said. I made my peace with that record. It never made its peace with me.
Will you hear us play?
First time I heard it slowed down, I sat in a parking lot and cried. Sixty-one beats a minute. I could finally hear what I played. In '67 I was going too fast to listen.
One set. Go slow. I'm listening.

afterWin.t: The lot does not clap after your set. It honks. Forty horns, low and long, like a congregation saying amen with its cars.
Mm-hm.
From Deacon, that is a standing ovation.
Wendell. Come with us. Front seat's mine, but I'll let you sit right behind me.
No, ma'am. I got a choir to count in next Sunday. And the Sunday after that.
But he gets out of the car, slow, and walks around to the open trunk, and lifts out a bundle wrapped in a purple choir robe.
Hold this for me, Pocket. Mind the rim.
Item five. Calfskin snare head. Pencil inside the rim: 'W.A. 12/31/67 - we was here.'
Somebody just put a snare drum back in me. Two and four. I had forgotten I had them.
That's all I'm giving. Except this. Professor left in '69. Ask Dess why.
He's been keeping that in the trunk twenty years. Under the spare. Wouldn't even let me look at it.

afterLose.t: Not yet. Sunday comes back around.
Trunk's still open. Run it back.

gigs.title: The Producers' Pledge
gigs.blurb: A producer who has flipped the break forty times finds out there's a grandmother inside it.

challenge.text: Everybody on the credits: play this set with at least 2 people.

before.t: Atlanta. August. A whole street closed off with sawhorses, smoke off six grills, and a sound system stacked on a porch so high the house looks like it's wearing it.
Here I run at seventy and at one-forty at the same time. Atlanta likes to have it both ways. So do I.
I got a cousin in Atlanta. Sells wings out of an old hearse. Says business is dead, but it's steady.
Y'all are the van! The roll call van! Oh no. Oh, I owe somebody money.
Decibel is twenty-two, in a sun visor, with a laptop open on an ironing board, which she says is the best stand money can't buy.
Okay. So. I have flipped that break forty times. Chopped it, pitched it, put it under every hi-hat in this zip code.
And then the roll call comes up on my phone. There's a grandmother inside the sample? I flipped it forty times and never once asked who's in it.
It's like borrowing somebody's car for six years and finding their baby seat in the back.
The laugh is our grandmother.
Wendell said ask Dess. So ask Dess, baby. Don't wait on Sunday.
You step behind the porch, away from the speakers, and call Harlem on a Thursday. She picks up on the second ring. She always picks up on the second ring.
Nana. Deacon said to ask you why the Professor left.
Ask me in person, Pocket. Not on a phone.
Click.
...So that went great. Come on. Come play. I'll be on the ironing board.

afterWin.t: After your set, Decibel climbs up on the porch rail with a microphone and a great deal of confidence about the rail.
Producers! I know y'all are out here. I see you with your little headphones around your neck.
Everybody who ever flipped those four bars: from now on, five names go in your credits. Deacon. Low. Sister. Professor. Dess. Every record. Call it the Producers' Pledge.
I know they're nicknames. It's a start. You don't wait to learn somebody's whole name before you say thank you.
You know Lantern's going to come after that.
Let 'em come. My mama's scarier than their lawyers.
She posts it from the rail. It is pulled down in fifty-one minutes. Lantern is fast. Lantern has lawyers who do not sleep.
BY THE END OF THE WEEK
Four hundred and six. Four hundred and six new records with the five nicknames in the credits. I'm counting. I'm going to keep counting.
They can pull a video. They can't pull four hundred songs.
I have been in the small print plenty. This is the first time the small print was about me.
Cross reads the list over Tuesday's shoulder and does not say anything for a long time.

afterLose.t: Run it back. I've flipped worse.
Seventy or one-forty, I'll wait at either speed. Again.

gigs.title: The Kindest Door
gigs.blurb: An open-air bass show on the beach, and the woman who owns the microphone has flown in to watch.

vibe.label: Miami bass, dance and Caribbean sound

challenge.text: Earn the encore on the sand: 13 stars over the set.

before.t: MEANWHILE, HARLEM
Odessa Fontaine's kitchen. A kettle, the two good cups, the radio off. A woman in a cream suit with a gold lantern on her lapel sits exactly where she was asked to sit.
You keep a beautiful kitchen, Mrs. Fontaine. 'She looketh well to the ways of her household.'
Drink your tea, Miss Lark. It's getting cold. So am I.
The whole country has heard your laugh this summer. The house would like to do right by you, before other people decide what right means.
You signed, Mrs. Fontaine.
I was nineteen.
You were paid.
I was nineteen.
Vivienne Lark sets an envelope beside the sugar bowl, squares it with one finger, thanks her hostess for the tea, and sees herself out.
Odessa waits until the door closes. Then she tears the envelope neatly in half, like a ticket, and puts both halves in the drawer with the rubber bands.
Miami. The sand still warm at nine at night, a sound system as tall as a lifeguard tower, and the ocean keeping time behind it.
Bonswa, bonswa! Come, stand here. No, closer. Closer. You feel that?
Bass is a hug you feel in your teeth.
Lantern's here. By the soundboard. The man with the folder from D.C., and a woman in a cream suit who has not sat down once.
Let them watch.

afterWin.t: The sand gives you an encore whether you asked for one or not. When you come off, the woman in the cream suit is waiting at the side of the stage, shoes in hand, so as not to ruin them.
Vivienne Lark. I run Lantern. I believe you've spent the summer looking for my family's paperwork.
We've spent it looking for the people your family's paperwork left out.
Fair. Watch Night 60 goes around the world this fall and comes home to Midtown on the night itself. I would like {band} to open it. Every date.
Why us?
You want those names heard? I own the microphone. Come and stand near it.
Four hundred people draw a paycheck from that story. Eleven schools. Tell me which ones I close so five names can go on a label.
I am not your enemy. I am the kindest door you will ever be shown.
Whitlock steps out of the dark beside her and hands Tuesday a folder. Tuesday puts her gloves on before she takes it.
Terms, for your consideration. There's no rush. There is a deadline.
We'll think on it, Miss Lark.
Please do. 'To every thing there is a season.' Mine closes at midnight on Watch Night.

afterLose.t: The sea doesn't stop for anyone. Neither do we. Again.
The tide comes back in. So can you. Run it back.

afterChallenge.t: Twelve-thirty, Watch Night, 1967. Nobody in that back room had a song. They had a hymn, and twenty-two minutes.
Dess hummed her mother's tune the way she had heard it at eleven o'clock: C.F.'s way, not the way the hymnal printed it.
The Professor sat on the organ bench with a sheet of manuscript paper on his knee and wrote in pencil, because pencil can change its mind.
At the top he wrote 'WATCH NIGHT'. Under it, after a moment: 'arr. by all of us'.
Ruth heard the hymn through twice and said, 'Put a backbeat under it.' Nobody argued. It was a new year. Everything was allowed.
Low found the root on his second try and grinned like he had found a dollar in his coat.
Deacon took a dime out of his pocket and tuned his own snare with the edge of it, a quarter turn at a time, until it sounded like somebody knocking on a door.
The Professor added one more line: 'tune: Dess's mama's hymn - 12/31/67'. Dess read it upside down from across the room and did not say anything. She did not have to.
